bib.title: Software Engineering for Machine Learning: A Case Study
bib.venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (ICSE-SEIP)

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Software Engineering for Machine Learning: A Case Study", Saleema Amershi, Andrew Begel, Christian Bird, Robert DeLine, Harald Gall, Ece Kamar, Nachiappan Nagappan, Besmira Nushi, Thomas Zimmermann. Microsoft Research, plus Gall at the University of Zurich. Year 2019.

Venue: the extracted text does not name a venue or a year, so I cannot confirm ICSE-SEIP 2019 from this file. Your task statement gives that venue. The latest reference date in the text is "accessed: 2018-09-24" (refs [10] and [12]), so the paper is consistent with a 2019 date.

COVERAGE: 59,283 of 59,283 chars, all 10 pages, including references. Nothing was skipped. The text was clean and not scanned. Fig. 1 and Fig. 3 are images, so only their captions were read. I did not run the figures script.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: The study had two phases. The first was 14 interviews. The second was a survey sent to 4195 members of internal AI/ML mailing lists, which 551 software engineers answered.
  number: 14 interviews; 4195 sent; 551 responses; 13.6% response rate
  setup: Microsoft only. Interviewees were chosen by snowball sampling and were mostly senior leaders. The survey was open-ended and used card sorting for free-text answers.
  quote: "We sent the questionnaire to 4195 members of internal mailing lists on the topics of AI and ML. 551 software engineers responded, giving us a 13.6% response rate."
  where: p.3, Sec. III.B

- claim: The respondents were mixed by role and mostly individual contributors.
  number: Data and applied science 42%; software engineering 32%; program management 17%; research 7%; other 1%; 21% managers; 79% individual contributors
  setup: the 551 survey respondents
  quote: "Data and applied science (42%), Software engineering (32%), Program management (17%), Research (7%), and other (1%). 21% of respondents were managers and 79% were individual contributors"
  where: p.3, Sec. III.B

- claim: The ML workflow has nine stages, with feedback loops. Some stages are data-oriented and some are model-oriented.
  number: 9 stages
  setup: a workflow Microsoft uses, related to TDSP, KDD and CRISP-DM. Fig. 1 is drawn linearly for simplicity.
  quote: "Some stages are data-oriented (e.g., collection, cleaning, and labeling) and others are model-oriented (e.g., model requirements, feature engineering, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring)."
  where: p.2, Fig. 1 caption; Sec. II.B
  The nine stages, in order:
  1. Model requirements: decide which features are feasible with ML and which model types fit.
  2. Data collection: find and integrate datasets, or collect new ones. Transfer learning from generic data is common.
  3. Data cleaning: remove inaccurate or noisy records.
  4. Data labeling: assign ground-truth labels, using engineers, domain experts or crowd workers.
  5. Feature engineering: extract and select features. Often blended with training for CNNs.
  6. Model training: train and tune.
  7. Model evaluation: use test or safeguard datasets with pre-defined metrics, plus human evaluation for critical domains.
  8. Model deployment: deploy the inference code to target devices.
  9. Model monitoring: monitor continuously for errors in real-world execution.
  
  Feedback loops: "model evaluation and monitoring may loop back to any of the previous stages", and training may loop back to feature engineering. The example given is a distribution shift between training and real-world data, which sends the team back to collecting more representative data.

- claim: Data availability, collection, cleaning and management is the top-ranked challenge at every experience level. It is the single largest share of the high-experience group's responses.
  number: rank 1 in the low, medium and high buckets; +60% frequency for high versus low; -2% for medium versus low
  setup: Table II, N=308 respondents with years-of-AI-experience data, split into low, medium and high at the 33rd and 67th percentiles
  quote: "Data Availability, Collection, Cleaning, and Management -2% 60% 1 1 1"
  where: p.5, Table II

- claim: Challenge importance shifts with experience. Education and training falls sharply. Tooling, scale and model evolution, evaluation and deployment rise sharply.
  number: Education and Training -69% (medium) and -78% (high), rank 1, 5, 9. AI Tools +144% and +193%, rank 9, 3, 2. Scale +154% and +210%, rank 10, 4, 3. Model Evolution, Evaluation, and Deployment +137% and +276%, rank 15, 6, 4. Integrating AI into larger systems -49% and -62%, rank 5, 16, 13.
  setup: same as Table II. Frequency is the change versus the low bucket.
  quote: "Model Evolution, Evaluation, and Deployment 137% 276% 15 6 4"
  where: p.5, Table II

- claim: A logistic regression controlling for several experience variables found five significant coefficients.
  number: Education and Training -0.18 (p<0.02); Educating Others +0.26 (p<0.01); tool issues +0.13 with team AI experience (p<0.001); end-to-end pipeline support and specifications each positively correlated with formal education (p<0.01 and p<0.03)
  setup: controls were personal AI experience, team AI experience, overall work experience, number of concurrent AI projects, and formal ML education
  quote: "Education and Training was negatively correlated with personal AI experience with a coefficient of -0.18 ( p < 0.02)"
  where: p.5, Sec. V.G

- claim: The maturity model has six dimensions, each rated per workflow stage. They are loosely based on CMM and Six Sigma. The authors call it descriptive, not prescriptive, and say it has no defined levels yet.
  number: 6 dimensions (S1 to S6), Likert 1 to 5
  setup: each respondent rated only the two stages they spent the most hours on
  quote: "a maturity model with six dimensions evaluating whether each workflow stage: (1) has defined goals, (2) is consistently implemented, (3) documented, (4) automated, (5) measured and tracked, and (6) continuously improved."
  where: p.5, Sec. VI
  
  Statement wording:
  - S1: "My team has goals defined for what to accomplish with this activity."
  - S2: "My team does this activity in a consistent manner."
  - S3: "My team has largely documented the practices related to this activity."
  - S4: "My team does this activity mostly in an automated way."
  - S5: "My team measures and tracks how effective we are at completing this activity."
  - S6: "My team continuously improves our practices related to this activity."
  
  Quote on intent: "Rather than being prescriptive (i.e., do this to get to the next maturity level), our intention was to be descriptive". The paper also says "More work is needed to define maturity levels similar to CMM." CMM's five levels, as cited in Sec. II.D, are initial (ad hoc), repeatable, defined, capable (quantitatively measured) and efficient (deliberate process improvement).

- claim: The Activity Maturity Index (AMI) is the mean of S1 to S6. It correlates with self-rated Activity Effectiveness (AE).
  number: Spearman correlation 0.4982 to 0.7627, all p<0.001
  setup: AE is a 1 to 5 self-rating. The authors take the correlation as validation. There is also an Overall Effectiveness (OE) score on a 1 to 5 scale.
  quote: "The Spearman correlation between the Maturity Index and the Effectiveness was between 0.4982 and 0.7627 (all statistically significant at p < 0.001) for all AI activities."
  where: p.6, Sec. VI

- claim: OE differs across application domains, which the authors treat as evidence the metric can separate teams by maturity.
  number: nine domains split into two groups, A to F and G to I. No effect sizes are given.
  setup: ANOVA and Scott-Knott test. Fig. 3's y-axis labels are elided for confidentiality, and domains are anonymized.
  quote: "An ANOVA and Scott Knott test identified two distinct groups to the OE metric, labeled in black (A–F) and red (G–I)."
  where: p.6, Fig. 3 caption

- claim: Three aspects make AI different from earlier software domains.
  number: 3 differences
  setup: the authors' synthesis from interviews and survey
  quote: "1) discovering, managing, and versioning the data needed for machine learning applications is much more complex and difficult than other types of software engineering, 2) model customization and model reuse require very different skills than are typically found in software teams, and 3) AI components are more difficult to handle as distinct modules than traditional software components — models may be “entangled” in complex ways and experience non-monotonic error behavior."
  where: p.1, abstract
  
  Details from Sec. VII:
  - Data: datasets rarely have explicit schemas. "the data schema (and the data) change frequently, even many times per day." Gebru et al. datasheets and the Datadiff tool are cited as aids.
  - Reuse: a model is not a function you edit. Retraining "can take as much work and expertise as the original model’s authors put in."
  - Modularity: entanglement can cause non-monotonic error propagation. Improving one part can decrease overall quality.

- claim: Best practices reported by teams, in six areas. None is quantified.
  number: none
  setup: respondent opinions from the survey and interviews, Microsoft only
  where: pp.3-5, Sec. V.A to V.F
  1. End-to-end pipeline support
     quote: "rock solid, data pipeline, capable of continuously loading and massaging data, enabling engineers to try out many permutations of AI algorithms with different hyper-parameters without hassle."
     Pipelines are automated for training, deployment and product integration. Rich dashboards help. Internal infrastructure named is AEther.
  2. Data management
     - Reuse data to cut duplicated labeling effort.
     - Blend data-management tools with ML frameworks.
     - Version data, and tag provenance on both models and datasets.
     quote: "Each model is tagged with a provenance tag that explains with which data it has been trained on and which version of the model. Each dataset is tagged with information about where it originated from and which version of the code was used to extract it (and any related features)."
  3. Education and training
     - A twice-yearly internal ML conference.
     - Weekly open forums.
     - Mailing lists and forums with thousands of participants.
  4. Model debugging and interpretability
     - Use more interpretable models or visualization.
     - Apply layered, tiered modularization in multi-model systems to simplify error analysis.
  5. Evaluation and deployment
     - Combo-flighting, meaning flighting a combination of changes.
     - Multiple metrics on experiment score cards.
     - Human-driven evaluation for sensitive data categories.
     - Automated tests built from curated test sets, with a human spot-checking errors.
     - Automate training and deployment, and use common versioning repositories for ML and non-ML code.
     - Couple ML and non-ML sprints and standups.
  6. Compliance
     - Microsoft's AI principles are fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics.
     - Compliance is explicitly out of scope for the paper.

- claim: Most reported challenge-importance shifts are about growing experience, but some challenges persist. Data, pipeline support and collaboration stay at similar ranks across buckets.
  number: End-to-end pipeline support ranks 4, 2, 4. Collaboration and working culture ranks 5, 6, 6.
  setup: Table II
  quote: "We find similarly consistent ranking for issues around the categories of end-to-end pipeline support and collaboration and working culture."
  where: p.5

LIMITS
- Authors' concessions, quoted: "Some findings are likely to be specific to the Microsoft teams and team members who participated". The data are self-selected and self-reported. The maturity model "triangulated its measures against other equally subjective measures with no objective baseline." Future versions "should endeavor to gather objective measures of team process performance."
- The nine-stage workflow is one that some Microsoft teams use, and readers must map it to their own.
- The maturity model is a "first attempt". It has no defined levels or thresholds. It does not say what to do to move up.
- The response rate is 13.6%. N=308 for Table II, not 551, and the paper does not explain the gap. The survey's actual response counts per stage are not given. Fig. 3 has no axis values.
- Dated: the paper is from 2018 to 2019 and predates LLM and foundation-model workflows. It uses AEther and Azure ML Studio. Monitoring and drift get only a passing mention. There is no section on monitoring practices, no CI/CD for models, and no feature stores. The text reports no quantitative effect of any best practice on outcomes.

BUILDS ON
- CMM: Weber, Curtis and Chrissis 1994.
- Six Sigma: Alexander 2001.
- Workflows: TDSP (Microsoft doc), KDD (Fayyad et al. 1996), CRISP-DM (Wirth and Hipp 2000), Salvaris et al. 2018 (Microsoft AI Platform), Patel et al. 2008, Hill et al. 2016.
- Hidden technical debt: Sculley et al. 2015.
- Troubleshooting integrative AI: Nushi et al. 2017.
- Data science roles: Kim et al. 2016 and 2018.
- Agile and DevOps at Microsoft: Begel and Nagappan 2007; Murphy et al. 2013; Senapathi et al. 2018.
- Other: TFX (Baylor et al. 2017), Sridhar et al. 2018 (model governance), Polyzotis et al. 2017 (data management), Gebru et al. (datasheets, 2018).

CODE: none. The paper has no code.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.2): the nine-stage workflow with feedback arrows. Large arrows run from evaluation and monitoring back to any earlier stage, and a small arrow runs from training back to feature engineering. It is the quickest way to see the data-oriented versus model-oriented split.
- Fig. 2 (p.3): the questionnaire structure. It has three parts: demographics, challenges, and time per activity; then tools, effectiveness and maturity for the two top-time stages; then dream tools, best practices and comments.
- Fig. 3 (p.6): OE by application domain, with the axis removed. It has little value because it has no numbers.
- Table I (p.3) lists the 14 interviewees: nine managers and five non-managers, in search, conversation, vision, ML tools, speech, ads and other areas.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean. Figures are images, so only captions were read.
- No venue or year string appears in the extracted text, so venue is unconfirmed from the file.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF text.
